summary.heading: Newton's universal law of gravitation
summary.html:
$$F = G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2}$$
  • Every mass attracts every other mass. The force is always attractive and acts along the line joining the centres. $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ $\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{kg}^{-2}$.
  • The forces on the two masses are equal and opposite (Newton's third law), even when the masses are very different.
  • Inverse-square law: double the separation and the force falls to a quarter.
  • A uniform sphere (or one made of uniform layers, like a planet) acts on outside objects as if all its mass were at its centre, so $r$ is always measured centre to centre. Any object can be treated as a point mass when it is tiny compared with the separation.

summary.heading: Gravitational field strength and field lines
summary.html:
$$g = \frac{F}{m} = G\frac{M}{r^2}$$
  • Gravitational field strength at a point: the force per unit mass on a small test mass placed there (small, so it doesn't disturb the field). Units $\text{N kg}^{-1}$, the same as $\text{m s}^{-2}$: $g$ equals the free-fall acceleration.
  • At the surface of a planet of radius $R$: $g_0 = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$. Above it, $g$ falls with the inverse square of the distance from the centre.
  • Field lines show the direction of the force on a test mass; they always point towards the mass, never cross, and are closer together where the field is stronger. Radial around a planet; close to the surface, almost uniform (parallel, equally spaced).
  • Field strength is a vector: fields from two bodies add as vectors. On the line joining two masses they point in opposite directions, and cancel at one point (nearer the smaller mass).

summary.heading: Circular orbits and Kepler's laws
summary.html:
• An orbiting satellite is in free fall: gravity provides the centripetal force, $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. The satellite's mass cancels, so the orbital speed and period depend only on $M$ and $r$.
  • New for 2028 Deduce Kepler's third law (SL and HL): substitute $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$ to get
$$T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}\,r^3$$
  • This is not in the data booklet. Use $T$ in seconds.
  • Kepler's laws (patterns found in Tycho Brahe's data, later explained by Newton): (1) each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus; (2) the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so a planet is fastest when closest; (3) $T^2 \propto r^3$. In IB calculations orbits are circular.
  • A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator, in the same direction as the Earth spins, with a period of one day, so it stays above the same point.
  • Weightlessness in orbit: gravity on the space station is still almost 90% of its surface value. Astronauts float because they and the station are in free fall together, so there is no contact force on them.

summary.heading: Gravitational potential energy and potential
summary.html:
• $mg\Delta h$ only works where $g$ is constant. On planetary scales the zero is fixed at infinite separation.
  • Gravitational potential energy of a system: the work done to assemble it from infinite separation of its parts.
$$E_p = -\frac{Gm_1m_2}{r} \qquad V_g = -\frac{GM}{r}$$
  • Negative because the masses attract: energy is released as they come together. $E_p$ rises towards zero as they separate.
  • Gravitational potential $V_g$ at a point: the work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity to that point. Units $\text{J kg}^{-1}$; a scalar, always negative, zero at infinity. $E_p = mV_g$.
  • Work done moving a mass: $W = m\Delta V_g$. Moving away from a planet, $\Delta V_g$ is positive, so work must be done. The work doesn't depend on the path (gravity is conservative).
  • Potentials from several masses simply add (with their signs), with no vectors.

summary.heading: Potential gradient and equipotential surfaces
summary.html:
$$g = -\frac{\Delta V_g}{\Delta r}$$
  • Field strength = minus the potential gradient: the gradient of a $V_g$–$r$ graph gives $g$; the minus sign shows the field points towards lower potential (inwards).
  • Equipotential surfaces join points at the same potential: spheres centred on a planet; near the surface, where the field is roughly uniform, flat and equally spaced.
  • No work is done moving along an equipotential. Field lines are always perpendicular to equipotentials. Drawn at equal steps of potential, equipotentials are closer where the field is stronger.

summary.heading: Escape speed and orbital energy
summary.html:
$$v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}} \qquad v_{\text{orbital}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$$
  • Escape speed: the minimum speed at a point needed to reach infinity with no further energy input. Set the total energy to zero: $\tfrac{1}{2}mv_{\text{esc}}^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{r} = 0$. It doesn't depend on the object's mass or launch direction (ignoring air resistance).
  • Circular-orbit energies (derive them): $E_k = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, $E_p = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$, total $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$. So $E_k = -\tfrac{1}{2}E_p$ and $E = -E_k$.
  • A higher orbit is slower but has more total energy (less negative): rockets must supply energy to raise an orbit. Energy to reach orbit from rest on a non-rotating planet = $E_{\text{orbit}} - E_{p,\text{surface}}$.
  • Orbital decay: in low orbits, thin-air drag removes energy, so $E$ becomes more negative and $r$ decreases. In the lower orbit the satellite moves faster ($E_p$ falls by twice as much as $E_k$ rises). Denser air lower down makes the decay speed up until the satellite burns up; the ISS boosts itself regularly.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Measuring $r$ from the surface: add the planet's radius to any height, and square the distance from the centre.
  • Saying there's no gravity in orbit (astronauts float because they're in free fall).
  • Thinking a heavier satellite needs a different orbital speed or period.
  • Adding field strengths from two bodies as plain numbers instead of vectors.
  • Using hours or days in $T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$.
  • HL Dropping the minus signs in $E_p$ and $V_g$, or mixing up $V_g$ (in $\text{J kg}^{-1}$) with $E_p = mV_g$ (in J).
  • HL Using $mg\Delta h$ for large height changes: use $W = m\Delta V_g$.
  • HL Saying drag slows a satellite down: it loses energy, drops lower and speeds up.

Patterns and trends: Kepler found his laws without knowing why they worked. Give students the planet table (r and T) and ask them to find the pattern before showing $T^2 \propto r^3$.
Is a pattern in data a law, or does it only become a law once a theory explains it?
Theories: Newton's one equation explained falling apples, orbits and tides. What makes a theory that unifies many things more convincing than several separate rules?
Newton refused to say what gravity is. Does a theory have to give a cause to count as a theory?
Measurement: Why was $G$ so hard to measure, when $g$ is easy? Estimate the force between two 1 kg masses 10 cm apart and compare it with the weight of a grain of sand.
Cavendish 'weighed the Earth'. Trace the chain: how does knowing $G$ and $g$ give the Earth's mass?
Falsification: Uranus's wobble could have falsified Newton's law, but instead it led to Neptune. When should an anomaly make us doubt a theory, and when should it make us look for something missing?
Mercury's orbit drift was eventually explained by general relativity, not a new planet (Vulcan). How would scientists at the time have decided which explanation to pursue?

oracy.html:
Opinion line (whole class, 8 minutes): students stand on a line from "agree" to "disagree", then justify their place to someone standing far from them. Claim: "If the Sun suddenly collapsed into a black hole with exactly the same mass, the Earth would be pulled into it."

  • I'm standing here because …
  • I've moved, because …
  • That depends on …

Listen for: $F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$ depends only on the masses and the distance, which are unchanged, so the orbit stays the same, although the Earth would become dark and cold.

Is describing the same as explaining?: Newton's law predicts where Mars will be in 100 years. Does that mean we understand gravity? What would an explanation add?
Ask students for an everyday example where they can predict something without knowing why it happens.
How can something act at a distance?: Compare three pictures: a force across empty space, a field filling space, and curved spacetime. Which feels most like an explanation, and why?
If two models give the same predictions, is it meaningful to ask which one is 'real'?
Are classical and modern physics compati: NASA still uses Newton's gravity to plan missions. Is Newton's law false, approximately true, or true within limits?
Where does Newtonian gravity stop being good enough (GPS satellites, Mercury, black holes)? Who decides the cut-off?
What makes a prediction convincing?: Neptune was predicted before it was seen; Mercury's drift was known before relativity explained it. Should a prediction count for more than an explanation of known data? Why?
Could a successful prediction ever be a lucky accident? How would we tell?

videos.use: A home-built Cavendish torsion balance showing the tiny attraction between ordinary masses. Use it for the Measurement NoS idea and to show why $G$ is so hard to measure.

videos.use: A short opener on orbits as constant falling. Pause after his street interviews and ask students to answer the title question before he does.

videos.use: Extension for the ToK questions on action at a distance and on classical and modern physics: general relativity's picture of gravity as curved spacetime rather than a force.
